text:
A: Hello. Can you hear me?
B: Yeah. Lorraine. Wednesbury.
A: Tomasz. Exeter. You're the last one for me, I think.
B: Me too. Thank God. Sorry. Not you. Just all of it.
A: No, I understand. It's a lot of talking for one day. I don't talk this much in a week.
B: You don't look like you'd be quiet. With all them books.
A: The books are quiet. That's why I like them.
B: Fair enough. What do you do, then? You a teacher?
A: Everybody says teacher. No. Student, archaeology. And I work on a packing line in a food factory, evenings and weekends. Machine operator.
B: Oh, right. I was on machines. Sewing machines, industrial. Upholstery. Till it shut.
A: So you know. When it's going well, nobody talks to you, and you just listen to the machine.
B: That's it. That's exactly it. You can hear when something's not right before it goes.
A: Yes! Last week my machine was jamming all night, and I knew from the sound, before the alarm. The engineer didn't believe me. Then it jammed. Erm, I cleared it myself in the end. I'm the one who does that.
B: Bet they don't pay you for it.
A: No. They don't.
B: They never do. My supervisor, years back, she'd stand behind you with a clipboard counting. I told her where she could put her clipboard.
A: My checklist I fill in after, sometimes. So I'm not a good example.
B: Nobody does them proper. Do you miss it, when you're at the uni? Being on your own, I mean.
A: Erm. Yeah, a bit. At uni everyone is nineteen and talks very fast and very sure. I sit at the back. I'm thirty-seven. My wife earns, you know, much more than me, she's pharmacist. So sometimes I think, what am I doing. And then I go to a museum and look at some old pot and I feel okay again. That's not very sensible, I know.
B: No, it's sensible. Better than lying awake.
A: You lie awake?
B: Sometimes. Bills and that. The electric. Gary says I worry too much. He's probably right, but somebody's got to.
A: Mm.
B: ...Sorry, the dog. She's looking at the door again.
A: It's okay. Let her out.
B: She can wait two minutes. She's twelve, she's in no rush for nothing. Do you have a dog?
A: No. We rent. Maybe one day.
B: They're good company. When everyone's out. I talk to her more than I talk to Gary.
A: I talk to the laundry in the spare room. It doesn't answer, it's fine.
B: Ha. Is that what that was, behind you? In the picture? I thought it was a coat rack.
A: Clothes airer. Permanently. The room is half study, half laundry. I'm losing.
B: Same in ours. Here, what do you call a bread roll? Because there's a lad from Lancaster says barm.
A: In Polish it's bułka. In Devon I just say roll. I didn't know barm.
B: It's a bap. Don't let nobody tell you different.
A: Okay. Bap. I'll tell the Polish shop, they'll be confused.
B: Good. Do they do proper bread there, then, or —
